title: Writing your own iterators; helper functions in slices/maps/strings
summary: strings.Lines, strings.SplitSeq and slices.Values hand out iter.Seq values; small adapters such as Filter, Map and Take compose them into lazy pipelines that stop the producer as soon as the consumer is done.

examples.title: strings.Lines, SplitSeq and FieldsSeq over Turkish text

annotations.note: strings.Lines (Go 1.24) yields every line with its "\n", unlike bufio.Scanner, which strips it. The lines concatenate back to the exact input; trimming is your job when you parse.
TrimSuffix removes the newline Lines kept, and Cut splits once at the first ";". A CRLF file would still leave "\r" at the end of each line.
The Turkish case mapping turns i into İ, so simit prints as SİMİT. strings.ToUpper would give SIMIT.
SplitSeq yields the same pieces as strings.Split but never builds the []string. For three tags that's style; inside a loop over a large export it removes one allocation per line.
FieldsSeq splits on runs of Unicode whitespace, like strings.Fields. slices.Collect turns any Seq into a slice when you do need one.
Lines and SplitSeq are documented as single-use: the second pass over the same value yields nothing, hence 4 and then 0. Call strings.Lines again for a second pass; it's cheap.

examples.title: Filter, Map and Take as generic adapters, composed lazily

annotations.note: An adapter takes a Seq and returns a Seq. Filter's only real duty is the yield check: when downstream stops, it stops pulling from upstream.
Map changes the element type, so it needs two type parameters. This function-over-Seq shape is the one the standard library uses.

Take returns right after the n-th value and never pulls the next one. Its counter lives inside the returned func, so every range starts from zero; decrementing the captured n instead would make the Seq single-use.
The predicate prints a trace. It counts letters with RuneCountInString; len counts bytes, and len("ılık") is 6, so a byte check would let a four-letter word through.

Building the pipeline runs nothing. The range pulls one value at a time through Filter, Map and Take; after the second match, Take's return sends false back up the chain, so ıhlamur and kiraz are never checked.

examples.title: An All() method on your own collection, consumed by maps and slices

annotations.note: A plain unbalanced binary search tree: just enough structure to be worth iterating over.
The convention from package iter: a collection exposes All() returning a Seq2 of key and value. Callers never see nodes or pointers.

In-order traversal is three lines with yield in the middle. The bool result carries "stop" up the recursion, so one false from yield unwinds every level. A Java Iterator for the same walk needs a class with an explicit stack.
Inserting from a map gives a random order and a different tree shape on each run, yet the in-order walk is always sorted, so the output is deterministic.
break after plate 34: walk returns false at every level and no further node is visited.
All returns a standard Seq2, so maps.Collect, maps.Values and slices.Sorted work with no glue code. Byte order puts Iğdır (I) before İstanbul (İ).

use_cases: Parsing text line by line without building a []string: strings.Lines, SplitSeq, FieldsSeq, and the same functions in package bytes
All, Keys, Values or Backward methods on your own collections
Small adapters (Filter, Map, Take) over database rows, file lines or API pages, where stopping early saves real work
slices.Collect, slices.Sorted and maps.Collect at the end of a pipeline when you need a materialized result
strengths: Lazy and early-exiting by construction: Take(..., 2) stops the producer after two matches, which a chain of slice-returning helpers can't do
Everything meets at one type, iter.Seq, so your adapters, your collections and the standard library helpers plug into each other
A tree iterator is a recursive function with yield in the middle, where Java needs an Iterator class with an explicit stack; Python's generators are the closest match
weaknesses: The standard library has no Map, Filter or Take for iter.Seq as of Go 1.27, so every project writes or imports its own
Nested calls read inside out: Take(Map(Filter(src, long), upper), 2) names the last step first
Single-use iterators such as strings.Lines and SplitSeq look like reusable values; a second range silently yields nothing
iter.Seq has no error channel: a sequence that can fail needs a convention, such as yielding (value, error) pairs through a Seq2

pitfalls.title: Forgetting that strings.Lines keeps the line ending
pitfalls.detail: Each line ends in "\n" (except possibly the last), and a Windows file with CRLF endings leaves "\r\n". Trim before comparing or parsing.

pitfalls.title: Ranging twice over a single-use iterator
pitfalls.detail: strings.Lines, SplitSeq and iterators over readers are single-use. Call the function again for each pass, or collect once with slices.Collect.
pitfalls.bad: lines := strings.Lines(s); n := count(lines); for l := range lines { ... }
pitfalls.good: n := count(strings.Lines(s)); for l := range strings.Lines(s) { ... }

pitfalls.title: Keeping adapter state outside the returned func
pitfalls.detail: Variables declared in the outer function are shared by every range over the Seq. Declare counters and cursors inside the func(yield ...) so each loop starts fresh.

pitfalls.title: Measuring Turkish text with len
pitfalls.detail: len counts bytes: len("ılık") is 6, len("Iğdır") is 7. Use utf8.RuneCountInString for letters, or range over the string.

quiz.q: for line := range strings.Lines("a\nb"): which values does line take?
quiz.why: Lines keeps each terminating newline; the last line has none because the input doesn't end in one.

quiz.q: Take(Map(Filter(src, keep), f), 2) runs over a src with a million elements. How many does src produce?
options: All million, then Take keeps two
Only as many as needed until Take has its two values
quiz.why: Each value travels through the whole chain before the next is read, and Take's false stops src. Exactly two only if the first two both pass the filter.

quiz.q: lines := strings.Lines(text); a := count(lines); b := count(lines). What is b?
options: 0, because Lines returns a single-use iterator
quiz.why: The documentation says single-use; per package iter's convention, calling it again after it finished yields nothing.

quiz.q: Why does the tree's walk method return a bool?
options: So a false from yield stops the whole recursion, not just the current level
quiz.why: Without it, the parent call would carry on to the right subtree and call yield again after false, which panics.

further_reading.title: package iter: naming conventions, single-use iterators

body:
## Concept

Since Go 1.23 the standard library hands out sequences as `iter.Seq[V]` and
`iter.Seq2[K, V]`: `slices.Values` and `slices.All` over a slice, `maps.Keys` and
`maps.All` over a map, and since Go 1.24 `strings.Lines`, `strings.SplitSeq`,
`strings.FieldsSeq` (and their `bytes` twins) over text. At the other end,
`slices.Collect`, `slices.Sorted` and `maps.Collect` turn a sequence back into a slice
or map.

Writing your own takes two forms. A collection gets a method such as `All()` that
returns a Seq built around its internal walk. An adapter is a function that takes a
Seq and returns a new one (`Filter`, `Map`, `Take`). Adapters compose into lazy
pipelines: nothing runs until a `range` pulls, values travel through the whole chain
one at a time, and the first `false` from the consumer stops the producer.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: like `Stream.filter().map().limit()`, lazy and short-circuiting. Go has no
  stream type: adapters are plain functions over `iter.Seq`, and there is no parallel
  mode.
- Python: like `itertools` with generators: `filter`, `map` and `islice` over a
  generator. Go's `Take` is `islice(seq, n)`.
- JS/Node: close to iterator helpers (`.filter().map().take()`) or a Node stream
  pipeline, but synchronous and without backpressure: the consumer's loop drives
  everything.
- C++: C++20 `std::views::filter | transform | take` composes lazily the same way.

## Design notes

Expose iteration through methods that return `iter.Seq` or `iter.Seq2`, named after
what they walk (`All`, `Keys`, `Values`, `Backward`, or a domain name like `Cities`).
Document single-use iterators, as `strings.Lines` does. Inside every iterator and
adapter, check `yield` and keep mutable state inside the returned function. Keep
adapters few and boring; three or four cover most needs, and when the standard library
already has a function (`slices.Collect`, `slices.Sorted`, `maps.Collect`), use it at
the end of the pipeline. Go 1.27's generic methods would let you wrap a Seq in your
own type and chain `.Filter(...).Map(...)` left to right, but the standard library
stays with functions over `iter.Seq`, which work with every sequence without
wrapping. For text, remember the Turkish rules from earlier lessons: count letters with
`utf8.RuneCountInString`, and change case with `unicode.TurkishCase`.
